content:
**Five longest rivers in the world – source locations and their elevations**

| Rank (by length) | River (total length ≈) | Primary source (name) | Elevation of source* | Typical reference |
|------------------|------------------------|----------------------|----------------------|-------------------|
| 1 | **Nile** (≈ 6 650 km) | **Lake Victoria** (the lake that feeds the White Nile) – the lake’s outlet at Jinja, Uganda | **1 135 m** above sea level | <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nile> |
| 2 | **Amazon** (≈ 6 400 km) | **Nevado Mismi** (Andes, Peru) – the Carhuasanta stream that becomes the Apurímac River, the most‑distant head‑water of the Amazon basin | **≈ 5 597 m** (≈ 5 600 m) above sea level | <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_River> |
| 3 | **Yangtze** (≈ 6 300 km) | **Tanggula Mountains** (Qinghai‑Tibet Plateau) – source of the Tuotuo (Ulan Moron) River, the uppermost reach of the Yangtze | **≈ 5 170 m** above sea level | <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yangtze> |
| 4 | **Mississippi‑Missouri system** (≈ 6 275 km) | **Brower’s Spring** (Centennial Mountains, Montana, USA) – the furthest head‑water of the Missouri River, which together with the Mississippi gives the longest river system in North America | **≈ 760 m** (2 500 ft) above sea level | <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_River#Source> |
| 5 | **Yenisei** (≈ 5 539 km) | **Sayan Mountains** (southern Siberia) – the head‑waters of the **Great Yenisei (Bolshoy Yenisey)** that join the **Little Yenisei (Maly Yenisey)** near Kyzyl. The most‑distant point is the source of the Bolshoy Yenisey on the southern slopes of the Sayan range. | **≈ 1 640 m** (≈ 5 380 ft) above sea level | <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yenisei_River> |

\*Elevations are given in metres above mean sea level (rounded to the nearest whole metre where appropriate).  

### Brief notes on each source  

| River | Why this source is considered the “source” |
|------|--------------------------------------------|
| **Nile** | The Nile has two major tributaries (White and Blue). The White Nile’s most remote head‑water is the Kagera River, but the internationally‑recognised source of the Nile system is the outlet of **Lake Victoria**, the lake that feeds the White Nile. |
| **Amazon** | The Amazon’s length depends on which head‑water is taken as the start. Modern hydrographic studies identify the **Carhuasanta stream** that originates on the slopes of **Nevado Mismi** (≈ 5 600 m) as the farthest source. |
| **Yangtze** | The uppermost stretch is the **Tuotuo River** (Ulan Moron) that rises in the **Tanggula Mountains** of the Tibetan Plateau, at roughly 5 170 m. |
| **Mississippi‑Missouri** | The Mississippi’s ultimate source is often given as **Lake Itasca** (463 m). However, when measuring the *entire* river system, the furthest head‑water is **Brower’s Spring** in Montana (≈ 760 m), the source of the Missouri River. |
| **Yenisei** | The Yenisei begins as two principal tributaries. The **Great Yenisei** (Bolshoy Yenisey) starts high in the **Sayan Mountains**; its most remote head‑water is on the southern slope of the range at about 1 640 m. The two tributaries meet near Kyzyl, after which the river is simply called the Yenisei. |

### How the data were gathered  

* River lengths and source locations were taken from the respective Wikipedia articles (the most widely‑cited baseline for geographical facts).  
* Elevations were taken from the “Source elevation” fields in those articles or, where not listed directly, from the elevation of the named mountain/lake/ spring as given in the article’s topography sections.  
* All elevations are reported in **metres** (the standard SI unit for altitude).  

If you need more precise figures (e.g., GPS‑derived elevations) or additional context—such as the historic debate over the Nile’s “true” source or alternative definitions of river length—just let me know!
